def: misrepresenting someone's argument as a weaker or more extreme version, then attacking that distorted version instead
scenario: Maria suggests the office cut back on printing. Her coworker replies, "So you want us to stop using paper entirely and email everything, even signed contracts?"
fix: Restate the other person's actual claim in words they would agree with before responding to it.

tests.s: When Kwame said kids should get a little less homework, his neighbor answered, "Oh, so you think school shouldn't teach anything at all?"
Priya proposed adding one vegetarian dish to the cafeteria menu. A classmate told everyone she was trying to ban meat from campus.

def: attacking the character or traits of the person making an argument instead of addressing the argument itself
scenario: At a town meeting, Diego presents traffic data supporting a new crosswalk. Another resident says, "Why listen to him? He can't even keep his lawn mowed."
fix: Ask whether the personal remark has anything to do with whether the claim is true; usually it doesn't.

tests.s: Hannah points out a math error in the team budget, and a colleague responds that nobody should listen to someone who is always late to meetings.
A scientist presents data on river pollution, and a critic dismisses it by calling her rude and arrogant without ever mentioning the data.

def: presenting only two choices as if they were the only possibilities, when other options actually exist
scenario: "Either we cancel the company picnic or we go over budget," Liam says, ignoring the option of a cheaper venue.
fix: Ask whether other options, including combinations or middle paths, were left out.

tests.s: A coach tells his players, "You're either fully committed to this team, or you don't care about it at all."
An ad warns homeowners, "Buy our alarm system, or leave your family unprotected."

def: claiming that one small step will inevitably set off a chain of events ending in disaster, without showing why
scenario: "If we let students use calculators on one quiz, soon they'll use them on every test, forget basic math, and fail in college."
fix: Check each link in the predicted chain and ask what evidence shows one step must lead to the next.

tests.s: Yuki's dad says that if she stays up late this one Friday, she'll start skipping sleep every night, fail her classes, and never get into college.
A council member warns that allowing one food truck downtown will lead to dozens more, then to every restaurant closing, then to an empty, dying city center.

def: treating a claim as true mainly because a famous or respected person said it, especially outside their expertise
scenario: An actor who plays a doctor on TV recommends a vitamin in a commercial, and Jamal buys it because "a doctor said so."
fix: Ask whether the person is a genuine expert on this exact topic and whether other experts agree, then check the evidence itself.
note: Citing real experts on their own subject is reasonable; the problem is irrelevant expertise, or treating someone's status as proof.

tests.s: In a debate about tax policy, Malik ends the discussion by saying, "A Nobel Prize-winning chemist agrees with me, so I'm right."
A website claims a diet cures arthritis, and its only support is a quote from a famous physicist praising it.

def: arguing that something is true, good, or correct simply because many people believe it or do it
scenario: "Millions of people are buying this new digital coin, so it must be a smart investment," Tomás tells his sister.
fix: Remember that popularity shows what people believe, not whether it's true; look for evidence about the claim itself.

tests.s: "Everyone at school has this phone, so it has to be the best one," Aisha tells her parents.
A podcast host argues that a diet must work because it was the most searched diet online this year.

def: an argument whose conclusion is already assumed in its premises, so it offers no independent support
scenario: "This news site is trustworthy because it says it only publishes reliable stories."
fix: Ask what support exists for the claim that doesn't already assume the claim is true.
note: "Begging the question" traditionally names this fallacy; it does not originally mean "raising the question."

tests.s: "Olga is the best manager in the company because no one manages better than she does."
"You can trust my promise because I'm an honest person, and you know I'm honest because I always keep my promises."

def: drawing a broad conclusion about a whole category from too few or unrepresentative examples
scenario: After two of his flights on one airline were delayed, Wei declares that the airline is always late.
fix: Ask how many examples the conclusion rests on and whether they represent the whole category.

tests.s: Fatima met two rude shopkeepers on her first day in a new city and decided that everyone who lives there is unfriendly.
After his first two dates from an app were boring, Liam announces that everyone who uses dating apps is dull.

def: an irrelevant topic brought up to distract attention from the real issue being discussed
scenario: Asked why the project went over budget, the manager talks at length about how hard the team worked through the holidays.
fix: Notice when the conversation drifts and steer back: "That may be true, but how does it answer the original question?"

tests.s: When a reporter asks a company spokesperson about a product recall, she begins describing the company's charity work and its new logo.
Malik's roommate asks why he hasn't paid the electric bill, and Malik starts talking about how expensive groceries have gotten.

def: trying to win an argument by stirring up feelings like fear, pity, or guilt instead of giving good reasons
scenario: A fundraising letter shows photos of shivering puppies but gives no information about how donations are actually spent.
fix: Separate how the message makes you feel from the reasons it gives, and ask whether those reasons hold up.

tests.s: Instead of explaining why his grade should be changed, a student tells his professor how crushed his parents will be if he doesn't pass.
A salesperson tells Hannah that if she skips the extended warranty, she'll be heartbroken when her laptop dies and her family photos are lost forever.

def: continuing something because of the time, money, or effort already spent, even when quitting would be wiser
scenario: Jamal stays to watch a boring movie at the theater because he already paid for the ticket.
fix: Ignore what has already been spent and can't be recovered; judge only the future costs and benefits of each option.

tests.s: Priya has spent $3,000 repairing an old car that keeps breaking down, and she pays for another big repair because she can't bear to waste what she's already put in.
A company keeps funding a failing software project after five years, mainly because executives don't want the money already spent to have been for nothing.

def: believing a random outcome becomes more or less likely because of what happened in earlier independent trials
scenario: After a roulette wheel lands on red six times in a row, Diego bets heavily on black, convinced it is "due."
fix: Remember that independent events like coin flips have no memory; past results don't change the odds of the next one.

tests.s: Sofia flips a fair coin and gets heads five times in a row, so she tells her friend that tails is now almost certain on the next flip.
A lottery player avoids last week's winning numbers, sure they are now less likely to come up again in this week's random draw.

def: the tendency to seek out, notice, and remember information that supports what you already believe while dismissing the rest
scenario: Convinced his new running shoes make him faster, Kwame remembers every good run in them and forgets the slow ones.
fix: Deliberately look for the strongest evidence against your view and ask what would change your mind.

tests.s: Aisha believes her coworker dislikes her, so she reads every short email from him as cold and forgets the times he thanked her.
Sure that a certain stock will soar, Liam reads only the forums that agree with him and dismisses every critical analysis as uninformed.

def: the tendency, after learning an outcome, to believe you knew or could have predicted it all along
scenario: After the underdog team wins the final, Tomás insists he "always knew" they would, though he picked the favorite beforehand.
fix: Write down predictions before outcomes are known, then compare them honestly with what happened.

tests.s: When the stock market dropped, Olga told friends the crash had been obvious, even though she had bought more stocks the week before.
After a couple announced their breakup, several friends said they had seen it coming for months, though none had mentioned any concern before.

def: letting one positive trait, such as good looks or charm, color your judgment of a person's unrelated qualities
scenario: Because the new hire is friendly and well dressed, his manager assumes his reports must be accurate too.
fix: Judge each quality on its own evidence and ask whether the impressive trait is actually relevant.
note: The negative version, where one bad trait colors everything, is sometimes called the horn effect.

tests.s: Parents assume the school's star athlete must also be honest and hardworking, though they know nothing else about him.
Because a company's phones look sleek and stylish, Wei assumes its customer service and battery life must be excellent too.

def: the principle that two things occurring together, or rising and falling together, does not show one produces the other
scenario: A survey notes that people who own more books tend to earn more, and a blogger concludes that buying books will raise your income.
fix: Ask whether a third factor, a reversed direction, or chance could explain the link before assuming one thing drives the other.
note: A link can hint at a cause, but showing one usually takes experiments or careful controls.

tests.s: A survey finds that students who eat breakfast earn higher grades, and the principal announces that breakfast makes students smarter.
Countries where people eat more chocolate tend to have more Nobel Prize winners per person, so a website urges readers to eat chocolate to boost their intelligence.

def: relying on personal stories or isolated examples instead of systematic data to support a general claim
scenario: "My grandmother smoked her whole life and lived to 95, so smoking can't be that bad," says Malik.
fix: Ask what larger, carefully collected data show; one memorable story can't outweigh studies of thousands of people.

tests.s: Despite crash studies showing seatbelts save lives, Diego refuses to wear one because his uncle once survived a crash after being thrown from the car.
Large studies found a cold remedy does nothing, but Hannah keeps recommending it because her neighbor swears it cured her.

def: the number of people or cases a study examines; too few can make results unreliable or misleading
scenario: An app advertises that "90% of users lost weight," but its study included only ten people.
fix: Check how many cases a result is based on; small numbers can produce big swings by pure chance.

tests.s: A toothpaste ad announces that "4 out of 5 dentists recommend" it, but the fine print shows only five dentists were asked.
A poll of just 15 voters is reported on the evening news as showing which candidate the whole state prefers.

def: presenting only the facts or data that support your point while leaving out those that contradict it
scenario: A company's ad shows sales charts for its two best months, omitting the ten months of decline.
fix: Ask what the full data set looks like and what was left out, such as other time periods or studies.

tests.s: To argue that the town's streets are safe, a council candidate cites crime figures from the calmest month of the year and ignores the other eleven.
A hotel's website displays the twenty five-star reviews it received and hides the two hundred one- and two-star reviews.

def: the duty of the person making a claim to support it, rather than expecting others to show it is wrong
scenario: Yuki says a local lake has a monster in it, and when friends doubt her, she says, "Well, you can't prove there isn't one."
fix: Ask the person making the claim to provide evidence; doubting a claim doesn't require proving it false.

tests.s: Kwame claims his new supplement doubles memory and tells his skeptical friends it's up to them to show it doesn't work.
A user posts that a famous singer secretly owns his favorite pizza chain and insists critics must disprove it before he'll stop sharing it.

def: assuming that because one event followed another, the first event must have produced the second
scenario: Fatima's computer crashed right after she installed a game, so she blamed the game, though a failing hard drive was the real culprit.
fix: Ask whether there's a real mechanism linking the two events, and whether the second might have happened anyway.

tests.s: The lights went out in Liam's apartment right after he plugged in his new toaster, so he returned it, but the whole block had lost power.
A soccer fan wore a new jersey on Saturday, his team won, and now he insists the jersey brings victories.

def: dismissing criticism by pointing out that the critic is guilty of the same behavior, instead of answering it
scenario: When Olga's sister asks her to drive more carefully, Olga snaps, "You got a speeding ticket last year!"
fix: Remember that a critic's hypocrisy doesn't make their point wrong; respond to the criticism itself.
note: Latin for "you too." Closely related to whataboutism.

tests.s: When a teenager is told he spends too much time on his phone, he only points out that his mom checks hers at every meal.
A city council member criticized for missing votes responds only that her accuser missed even more votes last year.

def: protecting a broad claim from a counterexample by redefining the category so that the example no longer counts
scenario: "No real fan would leave a game early." "My cousin is a lifelong fan, and he left early." "Then he's not a real fan."
fix: Ask whether the definition was changed only to dodge the counterexample; if so, the original claim has been quietly abandoned.

tests.s: Wei says no serious chef uses store-bought pasta. Shown an award-winning chef who does, he replies that she can't be a serious chef, then.
"No genuine runner walks during a marathon," Sofia insists. Told that an Olympic marathoner walked part of a race, she says he isn't a genuine runner.

def: changing the standard of evidence or success after it has been met, so the demand can never be satisfied
scenario: Priya's boss said she'd get a raise if she landed three new clients. When she landed three, he said it would take five.
fix: Agree beforehand on what would count as success or proof, and point out when that standard keeps changing.

tests.s: Diego asked for proof that the new bus route was faster. When shown it saved ten minutes, he said it had to save twenty, every day for a full year.
A skeptic said he'd accept electric cars as practical if one could go 300 miles on a charge. When shown one, he said it must also recharge in five minutes.

def: arguing something is good or safe because it comes from plants or the wild, or bad because it is artificial
scenario: Aisha assumes an herbal supplement can't hurt her because it's made from plants.
fix: Remember that many natural things are harmful, like poisonous mushrooms, and many artificial ones are helpful; judge each by evidence.

tests.s: A shampoo ad promises the product is safe for babies simply because every ingredient is "all natural."
Malik says anything made in a lab must be worse for him than something that comes straight from a plant, so he avoids all artificial sweeteners.

def: treating two things as the same because they share some feature, while ignoring major differences in scale or kind
scenario: Hannah argues that forgetting to return a library book is as bad as stealing a car, since both involve keeping something that isn't yours.
fix: Ask how the two things differ in size, harm, and context, not just how they're alike.

tests.s: Kwame says jaywalking and drunk driving are equally serious because both are traffic violations.
A commentator says a restaurant with one minor health citation is no different from one that caused a food poisoning outbreak, since both "broke health rules."

def: a query built on an unproven assumption, so that any direct answer seems to admit that assumption
scenario: A reporter asks a coach, "Have you stopped favoring your star player?"
fix: Point out the hidden assumption and challenge it instead of answering yes or no.

tests.s: During a meeting, someone asks Olga, "Why do you always ignore customer complaints?" though she has never ignored one.
A survey asks shop owners, "How much has the new parking policy hurt your business?" with no option for "It hasn't."

def: arguing that something is right or best simply because it has been done that way for a long time
scenario: When Liam suggests online scheduling at the clinic, the office manager says, "We've used paper sign-in sheets for thirty years, so they're fine."
fix: Ask what reasons support the practice today, apart from how long it has existed.

tests.s: A school board member opposes a later start time, arguing that school has always started at 7:30 in this town, so that must be the right time.
Asked why the family recipe calls for boiling vegetables for an hour, Tomás's aunt says it must be correct because their family has made it that way for generations.

def: assuming a compromise between two opposing positions must be correct simply because it lies between them
scenario: One friend says the restaurant opens at 5 p.m. and another says 7 p.m., so Wei assumes it must open at 6.
fix: Judge each position on its evidence; sometimes one side is simply right and the halfway point is wrong.

tests.s: One engineer says the bridge can hold 10 tons and another says 2 tons, so the manager posts a 6-ton limit without checking either calculation.
Sofia's doctor says a medication is safe while an online forum calls it poisonous, so Sofia concludes the truth must be that it's "somewhat dangerous."

def: relying too heavily on the first number or piece of information you encounter when making later estimates
scenario: A car dealer first shows Jamal a $50,000 model, so the $35,000 car he sees next feels like a bargain.
fix: Form your own estimate from independent facts before hearing others' numbers, and question where the first figure came from.

tests.s: People first asked whether a city has more or fewer than 5 million residents later guess its population far higher than people first asked about 200,000.
Because the first salary mentioned in the negotiation was $40,000, Aisha countered at just $45,000, though similar jobs paid $60,000.

def: judging how common or likely something is by how easily examples of it come to mind
scenario: After seeing news coverage of a shark attack, Olga becomes afraid to swim in the ocean, though her daily drive is far riskier.
fix: Look up actual statistics rather than relying on the most vivid or recent examples you remember.

tests.s: After a week of headlines about a plane crash, Diego decides to drive across the country instead of flying, believing driving is safer.
Because she can easily recall several friends whose homes were burglarized, Hannah guesses that most homes in her city are broken into every year.

def: drawing conclusions only from the people or things that made it through some filter, ignoring those that failed
scenario: Noting that several famous tech founders dropped out of college, Malik concludes that dropping out is a path to success.
fix: Ask what happened to the cases you can't see, the failures that were filtered out, before drawing conclusions.

tests.s: Admiring the old houses in her town, Fatima concludes builders long ago did better work, not considering that poorly built old houses were torn down decades ago.
Looking only at investment funds still operating today, an analyst concludes funds generally do well, not counting the many that shut down after poor results.

def: making different choices depending on how the same information is worded, such as in terms of gains or losses
scenario: Patients are more willing to choose a surgery described as having a 90% survival rate than one described as having a 10% death rate.
fix: Restate the information the opposite way and see whether your decision still makes sense.

tests.s: Shoppers prefer ground beef labeled "80% lean" over the identical beef labeled "20% fat."
Students are more likely to sign up for a course when told 75% of past students passed than when told 25% of past students failed.

def: when a team's desire for harmony leads members to suppress doubts and reach a poor, unchallenged decision
scenario: Every member of a planning committee privately doubts the launch date, but no one speaks up because everyone else seems confident.
fix: Invite dissent openly, assign someone to argue the other side, and collect opinions privately before discussion.

tests.s: A hospital board approves an expensive new wing in one meeting; several members had serious concerns but stayed quiet so as not to seem disloyal to the director.
On a hiking trip, four friends all go along with a risky shortcut, each secretly worried but unwilling to spoil the upbeat mood by objecting.

def: the tendency to feel the pain of giving something up more strongly than the pleasure of an equal gain
scenario: Kwame refuses a coin-flip bet in which he would win $120 on heads and lose $100 on tails, even though the odds favor him.
fix: Compare outcomes in plain numbers and ask whether a gain and a loss of the same size truly deserve such different weight.

tests.s: Tomás feels miserable for days after losing $100 on a bad trade, though winning $100 the month before barely lifted his mood.
Offered an even-odds bet to win $150 or lose $100, Fatima turns it down because losing $100 would sting more than winning $150 would please her.

def: the tendency to underestimate how long your own tasks will take, even when similar past tasks ran late
scenario: Every year Aisha expects to finish her taxes in one evening, and every year it takes her a full weekend.
fix: Base estimates on how long similar past projects actually took, then add a buffer.

tests.s: A contractor promises a kitchen remodel in three weeks, as he did for his last ten jobs, every one of which took more than two months.
Liam tells his professor the paper will be done by Friday, though each of his last five papers took twice as long as he expected.

def: a hidden third factor that influences both things being studied, creating a misleading link between them
scenario: Ice cream sales and drowning deaths rise together, but hot weather drives both: people buy more ice cream and swim more.
fix: Ask what other factor could affect both things, and look for studies that measured and adjusted for it.

tests.s: A study finds coffee drinkers have higher lung cancer rates, but the coffee drinkers also smoked more; once smoking is accounted for, the link disappears.
Children with bigger shoe sizes score higher on reading tests, but that's because older children have both larger feet and more years of reading practice.

def: a distortion that occurs when the people or cases studied don't represent the larger population being described
scenario: A gym surveys its members at 6 a.m. and concludes that most people in town love early morning exercise.
fix: Ask how the participants were chosen and whether that process favored certain kinds of people.

tests.s: A poll on a gaming forum finds that 85% of respondents want video game classes in schools, and the forum reports this as national opinion.
To estimate how many books a typical resident reads, a researcher interviews only people walking out of the public library.

def: a real improvement in symptoms that comes from believing you are being treated, not from the treatment itself
scenario: Patients given sugar pills they think are painkillers often report that their pain has eased.
fix: Compare treatments against an inactive look-alike in blinded trials so that belief alone can't explain the results.
note: It mainly affects self-reported symptoms such as pain or nausea, not the underlying disease.

tests.s: In a trial, half the volunteers with headaches got an inactive pill, yet many of them said their headaches improved after taking it.
Malik feels much more alert after drinking what he thinks is strong coffee, though his roommate secretly served him decaf.

def: the principle that, among competing explanations, the one requiring the fewest assumptions is usually preferable
scenario: When cookies vanish from the jar, Hannah suspects her teenage son rather than a burglar who took only cookies.
fix: Prefer the simplest explanation that fits all the facts, but drop it if new evidence demands something more complex.
note: A rule of thumb, not proof: the simpler explanation is the better starting bet, not guaranteed to be true.

tests.s: When her car won't start on a freezing morning, Olga suspects a weak battery before considering sabotage by a neighbor.
Seeing a crop circle appear overnight, Wei concludes people made it with boards and rope rather than a spaceship, since that explanation needs far fewer assumptions.

def: judging an idea or practice as good or bad based on where it originated rather than on its current merits
scenario: Diego refuses to use a proven study technique because it was first developed for military training.
fix: Ask whether the idea's origin actually affects whether it is true or useful today.

tests.s: Priya argues that calling someone "nice" is really an insult, since centuries ago the word meant "foolish."
Sofia won't try a popular dish because it was invented by accident when a cook made a mistake, so she says it "can't be any good."

def: shifting between two different meanings of the same word within an argument to reach a misleading conclusion
scenario: "A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So a feather cannot be dark."
fix: Pin down what each key word means and check that it means the same thing every time it appears.

tests.s: "The sign said 'Fine for parking here,' so I figured it was fine to park here."
"Nothing is better than a long vacation. A cheap sandwich is better than nothing. So a cheap sandwich is better than a long vacation."

def: assuming that what is true of each part must also be true of the whole they make up
scenario: Every player on the all-star team is excellent, so Tomás assumes they will easily beat a squad that has practiced together for years.
fix: Ask whether the whole can behave differently from its parts because of interactions, combinations, or scale.

tests.s: Since chocolate, pickles, and garlic each taste great on their own, Aisha assumes mixing all three will make a great dish.
Because one person standing up at a concert gets a better view, Liam concludes that if everyone stood up, everyone would get a better view.

def: assuming that what is true of a whole must also be true of each of its parts or members
scenario: The university is world famous, so Olga assumes every professor there must be a world-class teacher.
fix: Remember that a whole's overall traits, like its average or reputation, may not apply to every member.

tests.s: The country has one of the highest average incomes in the world, so Malik assumes every family living there is wealthy.
A salad is healthy, so Wei assumes every ingredient in it, including the heavy creamy dressing, must be healthy too.

def: applying a rule or standard to others while exempting yourself or a favored case without good reason
scenario: Hannah says everyone must follow the no-phones-in-meetings rule, but checks hers because her messages are "different."
fix: Ask what relevant difference justifies the exception; if there is none, the rule should apply equally.

tests.s: Diego insists speeding is dangerous and reckless, but says it's fine when he does it because he's an experienced driver.
A manager requires every employee to submit receipts for expenses but exempts his own spending, saying he's "too busy for paperwork."

def: spotting a cluster or pattern in data after the fact and claiming it was meaningful or predicted all along
scenario: A reporter marks every case of a rare illness on a map, spots one neighborhood with several cases, and declares something there must be causing them.
fix: Ask whether the pattern was predicted before looking at the data, and how often similar clusters appear by chance.
note: Named for a joke about a man who fires at a barn, then paints a target around the tightest group of bullet holes.

tests.s: An investor tests 500 trading rules on past stock prices, finds the one that would have earned the most, and advertises it as a proven winning strategy.
After the season, a fan sifts through the schedule, notices his team won every game played on a date ending in 7, and declares the pattern meaningful.

def: the finding that people with little skill in an area often overestimate their own ability in it
scenario: After reading one article about investing, Jamal is sure he can outperform professional fund managers.
fix: Seek objective feedback and compare your results with skilled performers; the less you know, the harder your gaps are to see.
note: From a 1999 study by David Dunning and Justin Kruger. How large the effect is remains debated; some researchers argue part of it is a statistical artifact.

tests.s: After two chess lessons, Yuki is certain she could beat most players at the local club, though she can't yet spot basic tactics.
On a grammar quiz, the students who scored lowest predicted they had outscored most of the class.

def: ignoring how common something is in general when judging the probability of a specific case
scenario: A test for a rare disease is 99% accurate. Tomás tests positive and assumes he almost certainly has it, forgetting that only 1 in 10,000 people do.
fix: Start with how common the thing is overall, then adjust for the specific evidence.

tests.s: Told that a stranger is quiet and loves books, Fatima guesses he is more likely a librarian than a salesperson, forgetting that salespeople vastly outnumber librarians.
An airport scanner wrongly flags 1% of innocent travelers, yet Sofia assumes anyone it flags is almost surely a smuggler, though smugglers are extremely rare among millions of passengers.

def: explaining other people's behavior by their character while underestimating the role of their circumstances
scenario: When a driver cuts him off, Kwame decides the man is a selfish jerk, never considering he might be rushing to a hospital.
fix: Before judging someone's character, ask what situation might lead a reasonable person to act the same way.

tests.s: When a new cashier is slow, Olga decides she must be lazy, not noticing that the register keeps freezing.
Diego assumes a classmate who skipped the study session doesn't care about grades, without knowing she works night shifts to support her family.

def: a preference for keeping things as they are, even when a change would leave you better off
scenario: Malik has stayed on the same expensive phone plan for eight years without ever comparing it with cheaper ones.
fix: Imagine choosing from scratch today: would you pick your current option?

tests.s: When a company switches its retirement plan from sign-up to automatic enrollment, participation jumps, because most workers simply stick with whatever the default is.
Priya keeps her savings in an account earning almost no interest, though a similar account at the same bank pays far more and switching takes five minutes.

def: the tendency for an unusually extreme result to be followed by one closer to the average
scenario: A flight instructor praises a student after an exceptionally smooth landing, the next landing is worse, and he decides that praise backfires.
fix: Expect extreme results to drift back toward normal on their own, and don't credit or blame whatever happened in between.

tests.s: A baseball rookie has a spectacular first season and a much more ordinary second one, and fans blame the pressure of fame.
A student who got the top score on one quiz scores closer to the class average on the next, and her teacher concludes she has stopped trying.

def: the tendency for journals to print studies with striking positive results more often than studies finding no effect
scenario: Twenty labs test whether a supplement improves memory; the two that find an effect appear in journals, while the eighteen null results sit in file drawers.
fix: Look for preregistered trials and reviews that include unpublished studies, and be cautious when only positive results appear.

tests.s: A doctor reviewing the journals finds that nearly every study of a new therapy shows benefits, unaware that many trials showing no benefit were never submitted or accepted.
Researchers who find no link between a food and cancer rarely get their papers accepted, so readers hear only about studies that do find a link.

def: the difference between a percentage change in the chance of harm and the actual number of people affected
scenario: A headline says a new drug cuts stroke risk in half, but the actual drop is from 2 in 1,000 people to 1 in 1,000.
fix: Ask for the actual numbers before and after, such as how many people out of 1,000 are affected.

tests.s: An ad claims a cream "doubles your chance of clear skin," but the fine print shows the chance went from 1 in 50 to 2 in 50.
A news story warns that a snack raises the risk of a rare cancer by 30%, without mentioning that the lifetime risk goes from 10 in 100,000 to 13 in 100,000.

def: a comparison set of subjects who don't receive the treatment, used to show whether the treatment made a difference
scenario: A company gives every employee a standing desk, sees productivity rise 8%, and credits the desks, without checking similar workers who kept their old desks.
fix: Ask "Compared to what?" and look for a similar set of people or places that didn't get the change.
note: Test scenarios for this concept show a conclusion drawn without one.

tests.s: A town installs new streetlights and burglaries fall 20%, but no one checks whether burglaries fell just as much in nearby towns without new lights.
A tutoring company reports that its students' scores rose over the school year, without comparing them to similar students who got no tutoring and also improved.

def: the difference between something required for an outcome and something that guarantees the outcome on its own
scenario: Oxygen is required for a fire, but oxygen alone doesn't start one; fuel and heat are also needed.
fix: Ask two questions: "Can it happen without this?" and "Does this alone guarantee it?"

tests.s: Aisha reasons that since a college degree is required for the job, anyone who has a degree is sure to be hired.
Jamal assumes that because he has a concert ticket, he is certain to get in, forgetting that the venue also requires photo ID.

def: the invalid pattern: if A, then B; B is true; therefore A must be true
scenario: "If it rained, the street is wet. The street is wet, so it must have rained," though a street sweeper had just passed.
fix: Remember that B could have other explanations; seeing the result doesn't prove the particular reason you had in mind.

tests.s: "If someone has the flu, they have a fever. Hannah has a fever, so she must have the flu."
"If the battery is dead, the car won't start. Wei's car won't start, so the battery must be dead."

def: the invalid pattern: if A, then B; A is false; therefore B must be false
scenario: "If you're a doctor, you went to college. Malik isn't a doctor, so he didn't go to college."
fix: Remember that B might still be true for other reasons even when A is false.

tests.s: "If it snows, school is canceled. It didn't snow, so school can't be canceled today."
"If you study abroad, you'll learn a new language. Sofia never studied abroad, so she can't have learned a new language."

def: the difference between conclusions guaranteed by their premises and conclusions that are only probable, drawn from observed patterns
scenario: "All mammals have lungs; whales are mammals; so whales have lungs" guarantees its conclusion, while "The sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow" makes it only highly likely.
fix: Ask whether the conclusion must be true if the premises are, or is merely likely based on past cases.

tests.s: Detective Kwame reasons that only two people had keys and one was abroad, so the other must have unlocked the door; his partner reasons the suspect has lied before, so she's probably lying now.
A math student proves a rule holds for every even number using definitions, while a scientist predicts a pattern will continue because it has held in every past observation.

def: the property of a claim that could, in principle, be shown wrong by some possible observation or test
scenario: Rafael says an invisible, silent dragon that leaves no traces lives in his garage, so nothing could ever show he's wrong.
fix: Ask, "What evidence would show this is wrong?" If nothing could, the claim can't be tested.
note: Associated with philosopher Karl Popper, who argued that scientific claims must be testable in this way.

tests.s: A fortune teller predicts, "Something important will happen to you this year," a claim no possible outcome could ever count against.
Hannah's uncle claims a secret society controls world events, and he treats every lack of evidence as proof of how well they hide.

def: the difference between reasoning whose conclusion follows logically and reasoning that also starts from true premises
scenario: "All birds can fly; penguins are birds; so penguins can fly." The logic is correct, but a premise is false, so the conclusion fails.
fix: Check two things separately: does the conclusion follow, and are the premises actually true?

tests.s: "All fish live in fresh water; tuna are fish; so tuna live in fresh water." The structure works, but the first statement is untrue.
A student writes a perfectly logical proof that the moon is made of cheese, starting from the premise that every round object in the sky is cheese.
